lectures.title: History of artificial intelligence · Part 1
lectures.subtitle: Foundations and the birth of AI
topics: The birth of AI and early learning systems
lectures.intro: The first part connects the ideas that made AI possible: probability, computation, artificial neurons and early learning systems.
takeaways: Explain how evidence can change a belief.
Distinguish a test of behavior from a claim about consciousness.
Connect early learning systems with examples and feedback.

lectures.title: History of artificial intelligence · Part 2
lectures.subtitle: From AI winters to generative models
lectures.intro: Build on the early foundations to follow changing expectations, renewed neural learning and the rise of modern generative models.
takeaways: Explain why AI progress includes setbacks as well as breakthroughs.
Distinguish rule-based expertise from learning from data.
Describe how data, computation and learning contribute to modern AI.
recap: Explain how evidence can change a belief.
Distinguish a test of behavior from a claim about consciousness.
Connect early learning systems with examples and feedback.

lectures.title: Search algorithms · Part 1
lectures.subtitle: Problem formulation and uninformed search
topics: States, paths, costs and the frontier
lectures.intro: Model a search problem, then compare exploration rules that do not use an estimate of the remaining distance.
takeaways: Represent a task using states, actions, a goal and costs.
Explain the difference between queue and stack exploration.
Choose an uninformed method using the costs and memory available.

lectures.title: Search algorithms · Part 2
lectures.subtitle: Heuristics and informed search
topics: A* and the conditions behind its guarantees
lectures.intro: Use estimates to guide exploration, then examine when the resulting search is complete or finds a cheapest route.
takeaways: Explain what a heuristic estimates.
Compare greedy search with the cost-plus-estimate rule in A*.
Use a valid bound to explain why a branch can be pruned.
recap: Represent a task using states, actions, a goal and costs.
Explain the difference between queue and stack exploration.
Choose an uninformed method using the costs and memory available.

lectures.title: Constraint satisfaction · Part 1
lectures.subtitle: Modeling, backtracking and propagation
lectures.intro: Translate a problem into legal assignments and remove impossible choices before doing more search.
takeaways: Name the variables, domains and rules in a simple problem.
Explain when backtracking rejects an assignment.
Distinguish local support from a complete solution.

lectures.title: Constraint satisfaction · Part 2
lectures.subtitle: Domain splitting and local search
topics: Split domains to complete the search
lectures.intro: Combine propagation with branching, then contrast systematic search with methods that repair complete assignments.
takeaways: Explain how splitting and propagation work together.
Compare building an assignment with repairing one.
Explain why a restart or a temporarily worse move may help.
recap: Name the variables, domains and rules in a simple problem.
Explain when backtracking rejects an assignment.
Distinguish local support from a complete solution.

lectures.title: Introduction to machine learning · Part 1
lectures.subtitle: Learning settings and applications
lectures.intro: Identify what a system learns from, what it predicts, and how different learning settings appear in practical tasks.
takeaways: Distinguish learning from examples from making a prediction.
Identify the learning signal in a familiar task.
Separate the learning setting from the application domain.

lectures.title: Introduction to machine learning · Part 2
lectures.subtitle: Data, models and generalization
lectures.intro: Work from a concrete dataset to a prediction model, then evaluate whether the learned relationship transfers to new cases.
takeaways: Distinguish observations, input features and targets.
Explain why a good training fit can fail on new cases.
Give training, validation and testing separate roles.
recap: Distinguish learning from examples from making a prediction.
Identify the learning signal in a familiar task.
Separate the learning setting from the application domain.

lectures.title: Regression · Part 1
lectures.subtitle: Fitting and evaluating prediction models
topics: Straight lines, residuals and least squares
lectures.intro: Fit numerical predictions and compare simple and flexible models using both training and held-out evidence.
takeaways: Interpret the intercept, slope and residuals of a line.
Explain what a fit score does and does not establish.
Recognize overfitting and underfitting from training and held-out behavior.

lectures.title: Regression · Part 2
lectures.subtitle: Uncertainty, inference and interpretation
lectures.intro: Explain how fitted models vary, quantify uncertainty, and interpret associations without confusing them with causal effects.
takeaways: Describe sensitivity to the training sample.
Distinguish statistical evidence from practical or causal conclusions.
Use residual patterns to motivate the next model check.
recap: Interpret the intercept, slope and residuals of a line.
Explain what a fit score does and does not establish.
Recognize overfitting and underfitting from training and held-out behavior.

lectures.title: Classification · Part 1
lectures.subtitle: Probabilities, Naive Bayes and logistic predictions
lectures.intro: Connect class probabilities to decisions, build a Naive Bayes model, and introduce the logistic probability curve.
takeaways: Distinguish a class probability from a certain outcome.
Explain the simplifying assumption in Naive Bayes.
Separate logistic probabilities from the threshold used to make a decision.

lectures.title: Classification · Part 2
lectures.subtitle: Fitting logistic models and nearest neighbors
lectures.intro: Continue from the logistic curve to its fitting objective, then compare neighbor methods and select a prediction procedure fairly.
takeaways: Explain why fitting rewards probability assigned to the observed label.
Predict a class or a number from nearby examples.
Explain why scaling and validation matter when choosing neighbors.
recap: Distinguish a class probability from a certain outcome.
Explain the simplifying assumption in Naive Bayes.
Separate logistic probabilities from the threshold used to make a decision.

lectures.title: Classification · Part 3
lectures.subtitle: Perceptrons and linear support-vector machines
topics: Linear boundaries and the XOR limitation
Margins, support vectors and soft-margin SVMs
lectures.intro: Learn a linear boundary, inspect its limitations, and use margins to distinguish among possible separators.
takeaways: Explain how a perceptron uses mistakes as feedback.
Recognize when a straight boundary is insufficient.
Explain the roles of margins, support vectors and allowed violations.

lectures.title: Classification · Part 4
lectures.subtitle: Feature maps and kernel support-vector machines
lectures.intro: Represent more complex boundaries with feature maps, then derive and apply the kernel form of a support-vector machine.
takeaways: Explain why an additional feature can simplify a boundary.
Describe the kernel trick as a feature-space similarity calculation.
Compare kernel flexibility and computational cost using validation.
recap: Explain how a perceptron uses mistakes as feedback.
Recognize when a straight boundary is insufficient.
Explain the roles of margins, support vectors and allowed violations.

lectures.title: Clustering and principal components · Part 1
lectures.subtitle: K-means and Gaussian mixtures
lectures.intro: Discover groups through centroids and mixture models, while checking how initialization, geometry and group count affect the result.
takeaways: Explain the assignment and mean-update steps of K-means.
Distinguish a tight fit from a useful choice of group count.
Explain soft membership and why convergence does not prove a global optimum.

lectures.title: Clustering and principal components · Part 2
lectures.subtitle: Hierarchical clustering, PCA and preprocessing
lectures.intro: Build nested groups, reduce the number of dimensions, and examine how preprocessing changes the structures you see.
takeaways: Read a dendrogram using its chosen distance rule.
Explain how PCA keeps directions of variation.
Describe how scaling and whitening affect interpretation.
recap: Explain the assignment and mean-update steps of K-means.
Distinguish a tight fit from a useful choice of group count.
Explain soft membership and why convergence does not prove a global optimum.
